content:
Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance. 

Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. The reports were sourced from a single academic institution; no external datasets were used for model development or validation. 

A multi-agent AI pipeline was developed comprised of the following components: (1) a rule-based agent using regular expressions (regex) designed to identify and label standardized anatomical sections (such as lungs, liver, kidneys, etc.) at the sentence level; (2) a locally hosted large language model (Llama 2 13B, fine-tuned on radiology text) for natural language parsing and sentence classification within the labeled sections; and (3) QA agents to detect discrepancies. Agents interacted sequentially, where each structured the output for downstream processing, with the QA agent flagging reports for review when potential issues were detected.

The QA process evaluated: (a) mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections or within sections (e.g., an abnormality described in the Findings, but not mentioned in the Impression, or vice versa); (b) gender-anatomy conflicts (e.g., reference to “prostate” in a report for a female patient, determined by matching patient-demographic fields to anatomical keywords in the text); and (c) undocumented communication of critical findings (flagged when phrases indicating urgent findings were present without corresponding documentation of communication in the report). 

A random subset of 45 reports (stratified by flagged issue) was selected for radiologist evaluation to mitigate selection bias. Two board-certified radiologists independently reviewed the restructured reports for fidelity to the original, accuracy of structuring, omission of clinically important content, and potential fabrication.

Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 (14.1%) reports, most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%). In the radiologist evaluation of the 45-report subset, both reviewers agreed that 31 reports (69%, 95% CI: 54–81%) were correctly restructured, 2 reports (4%, 95% CI: 0–12%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on the remaining 12 reports (27%, 95% CI: 15–41%). The Cohen’s kappa for inter-reviewer agreement was 0.49 (moderate agreement). Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. QA performance was scored per consensus as “excellent” (error-free, high clarity and structure), “good” (minor, non-clinically relevant issues), or “fair” (noticeable structuring deficiencies). Ratings for QA performance were “excellent” in 38%, “good” in 46%, and “fair” in 16% of evaluated reports. Descriptive 95% confidence intervals are provided for these proportions; formal hypothesis testing was not performed due to sample size.

Conclusion: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow. In a pilot radiologist evaluation of 45 reports, the system demonstrated favorable performance with moderate reviewer agreement. Limitations include a small sample for manual evaluation and use of a single-institution dataset; further validation is needed to assess generalizability and clinical impact. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice, but broader studies are required.

"""

A multi-agent AI pipeline was developed to perform report structuring and quality assurance (QA). The system structured the report into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regex rules and local large language models. It also detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections, or within sections; gender-anatomy conflicts; and undocumented communication of critical findings. Two board-certified radiologists independently evaluated a 45-report subset. Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 (14.1%) reports, most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%). In the radiologist evaluation, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%) were correctly restructured, 2 reports (4%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on the remaining 12 reports (27%). Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. REVIEW:
"""
- The descriptions of the multi-agent AI system and its components lack sufficient detail (e.g., specifics about “regex rules” and “local large language models” are missing); clarify the architecture, model types, and how agents interact to enhance reproducibility and understanding.

- The process for developing and validating the system is vague. Specify how the AI system was trained and validated, and whether any external datasets were used to assess generalizability.

- The criteria for the quality assurance (QA) process (e.g., how mismatches or “gender-anatomy conflicts” are determined) are not well-defined; provide concrete definitions and possibly examples to ensure clarity.

- The method for subset selection (45 of 638 reports) for radiologist evaluation is not described; detail how these reports were chosen to address potential selection bias.

- Inter-reviewer agreement metrics (e.g., kappa statistics) are not reported, despite disagreement in 27% of cases; add quantitative inter-rater reliability measures to strengthen the evaluation.

- The rationale for some outcome metrics is unclear (e.g., why “excellent/good/fair” ratings were chosen and how these were defined); clarify scoring systems and provide explicit criteria.

- Only descriptive statistics are provided; consider adding statistical analyses to compare performance (e.g., error rates, confidence intervals, or significance testing).

- The conclusion may overstate the findings given the limited (45 report) radiologist evaluation; temper claims and provide limitations, especially regarding sample size and assessment scope.
"""
